execution: Pedal the cycle ergometer under physiotherapist supervision twice a week. Table 1 describes 10 minutes of warm-up at 60–70% of test-measured maximum heart rate, four 4-minute work bouts at 90–95%, intervening 3-minute active recoveries at 70%, and a 3-minute cooldown at 60–70%. A heart-rate sensor monitored effort. Participants worked up to target intensity over the first two weeks. These are the trial parameters.
remainingGap: The paper defines a timed program. The training ergometer fit, cadence and method of varying resistance are unspecified. Equipment and workload increments used in the cardiopulmonary test cannot establish those training details.

execution: On a treadmill, walk or run for four minutes at 90–95% of measured maximum heart rate. Alternate the work bouts with three-minute active recoveries at approximately 70% maximum heart rate. The trial used four work bouts within a supervised session described as 40 minutes, with speed and effort adapted to each participant. The pilot also allowed a separate individually performed endurance session.
remainingGap: Walking and running are explicit alternatives. The intervention does not prescribe a single gait, speed, slope, or handrail contact. The Balke test in the protocol describes the fitness assessment.

execution: An instructor taught ten adapted forms drawn from the 108-posture Yang sequence. The forms progressively shift support from two legs toward one and increase trunk and arm turning. The instructor guide illustrates an hour comprising a five-minute welcome, ten-minute warm-up, thirty minutes of form practice and walking meditation, ten minutes of relaxation, breathing and meditation, and five minutes of review. The trial compared different class frequencies and durations.
remainingGap: The published protocol and instructor guide do not enumerate the ten forms or their complete order, footwork and transitions. They define a taught sequence, not ten independently validated movements.

execution: Use the trial’s conventional two-handed barbell lift. The plates rest on the floor with the bar close in front of the shins. Place the feet inside the hands, bend hips and knees to grip the bar and brace while holding neutral lumbar alignment. Extend hips and knees, keeping arms straight, until standing with the bar against the upper thighs. On the descent hinge the hips first, bend the knees as the bar passes them, and set the plates down. Release the bar and stand briefly before resetting. The trial monitored symptoms and individualized load.

execution: At each session the therapist checked the response to repeated movements or sustained lumbar positions and chose the direction that moved distal symptoms toward the spine. For an extension responder Table 3 offers lying prone, sustained elbow support, a press-up to elbows, a press-up to straight arms, a straight-arm press-up with sag, a press-up with overpressure, and repeated extension in standing. These are progression options selected according to symptom response.
remainingGap: The diagnosis alone cannot select direction, starting option, end range, progression or the need for therapist overpressure.

execution: Lying on the back, lift the head using the neck flexors against the weight of the head, then lower between repetitions. The 2003 endurance group performed three sets of twenty. A separate earlier study describes a slow lift of about 5 cm and a short hold on a training bench for its weakest patients. The 2003 report does not adopt this height or hold for its endurance arm.
remainingGap: The exact 2003 starting head support, chin alignment, lift endpoint and return cue are missing. A supported chin nod is a different task.

execution: The 2003 group sat to perform four elastic-resistance directions: straight forward, diagonally to each side, and straight backward. Load was set from measured isometric strength. The cited earlier forward demonstration shows a seated person facing away from a wall-bar anchor at head height, with an elastic band around the forehead. The trunk inclines from the hips while the neck and trunk stay aligned, rather than flexing the neck through a large arc. The earlier authors also describe reversing the pull for the extensors.
remainingGap: The 2003 report does not depict all four variants. In particular the head contacts, body orientation and anchor geometry for the diagonal directions are not established by the precursor figure. The case-specific resistance and four variants preclude one universal image.

execution: The guideline discusses progression from gentle neck isometrics to low-load endurance as tolerated. In Dedering’s radiculopathy protocol the physiotherapist examined the individual and selected specific exercises and doses from a progression framework. execution: Begin supine with head supported in neutral and jaw relaxed. In the initial unresisted stage the eyes follow imagined nodding, turning to either side, or looking up/back while the neck stays still. In the low-resistance stage, attempt a small nod against a hand at the chin, rotation against the hand at the temple, or extension by pressing the back of the head into its support. The manual shows a folded towel under the head. Sitting follows adequate supine control. The trial subsequently added individually progressed endurance work.
remainingGap: The family contains three directions, different resistance contacts and multiple stages. Each can be separately identified for review. The whole family cannot be illustrated with a single generic neck isometric.

execution: Lie on the opposite side on a flat surface, lower arm bent beneath the head as pictured, legs slightly bent for balance. Hold a dumbbell in the upper hand, elbow bent about 90 degrees and upper arm against the side with the elbow between hip and lower ribs. Start with the hand near the navel, low in front of the body. Keep the scapula slightly back and elbow fixed. Rotate the forearm upward as far as available, at most vertical, keeping the trunk still. Lower to just above the surface.

execution: Lie on the flat support with head, back and pelvis down, both knees bent to roughly 90 degrees and feet planted. Support one dumbbell over the working shoulder with the arm straight and vertical. Begin with the scapula resting on the surface. Keeping the elbow angle fixed and torso facing up, move that shoulder blade forward around the rib cage and reach the weight slightly higher. Lower the shoulder slowly, stopping before completely relaxing. Only the shoulder/scapula leaves the support.

execution: Use the two-part doorway option in the MOON nonoperative booklet. Stand facing the open doorway. Put a hand or forearm on each jamb at shoulder level, lean the body forward between the hands and hold. Ease back, place the hands or forearms higher than the head on the jambs, and lean forward again. The first part may also use the two walls of a corner. The study-era booklet shows a standing staggered stance as one example.

execution: For the Watson standing version, stand upright with the working upper arm by the trunk at zero abduction and elbow bent, holding an elastic band anchored across the body on the opposite side. Figure 3a shows a door-handle attachment near waist height and the elbow held at the side without a pad. Rotate the forearm away from the midline from neutral to a maximum of 45 degrees of external rotation per the trial table, then return under control without turning the torso. Scapular position and the effective arc were selected by the therapist. The authors demonstrate an additional scapula-resistance band in the figure when that correction is chosen.

execution: In the pictured rack, stand on both forefeet at the edge of a flat weight disc with heels free, knees straight and weight shared equally. Carry the barbell across the shoulders with a wide two-handed grip. Rise onto both forefeet, then lower the heels through the available ankle excursion with the knees still straight. The heavy-slow trial used three seconds in each direction. The paper individualizes load progression, and supplies no universal weight or ankle angle.
